Lorsqu’une demande de contrôle est formulée, l’espoir est que le contrôle révèle l’absence d’engin explosif improvisé dissimulé ou de tout autre article menaçant, et que l’envoi puisse être acheminé. Dans le pire des cas (lorsque l’envoi ne peut être chargé en raison d’un signalement non résolu), les effets sont limités à l’envoi en question (par exemple, à une boîte ou à une palette). Ils se feront généralement sentir à la suite d’une tentative de contrôle infructueuse (c’est-à-dire lorsque le contrôle ne peut exclure la présence d’un article menaçant). Dans ce cas, les équipes d’intervention d’urgence sur place prennent le relais et le problème n’est plus du ressort du CFAPC.

L’effet de la décision de ne pas charger un envoi se limite au vol à bord duquel de l’espace est réservé pour l’envoi et ne s’appliquerait que dans des circonstances où la menace d’un engin explosif ne peut être exclue. Si de nouveaux renseignements permettant d’annuler le signalement après le départ du vol sont communiqués, le fret sera traité comme un nouvel envoi dans le système et sera réintégré dans la chaîne d’approvisionnement en vue de son transport. La décision d’émettre un avis NPC n’a, à ce jour, jamais été prise et la probabilité qu’elle se produise reste faible. De ce fait, la probabilité de retards liés à un avis NPC est également limitée. La capacité des transporteurs aériens à fournir les données PLACI au CFAPC dès que possible avant le chargement du fret dans l’avion contribuera également à réduire les retards potentiels. De cette manière, les transporteurs aériens pourraient s’assurer qu’ils respectent leurs conditions de service pour le transport de fret et que l’effet des décisions de réduction des risques prises par le CFAPC reste limité.

En fin de compte, la décision d’appliquer une mesure d’atténuation des risques à un envoi est prise par les analystes du CFAPC dans un petit nombre de cas et peut prendre quelques secondes avant d’être approuvée ou annulée. Par exemple, un envoi peut être signalé pour examen par le système, puis autorisé par un analyste en quelques secondes, sans qu’il soit nécessaire de fournir des renseignements supplémentaires. Le changement d’état est communiqué au transporteur aérien dans le système immédiatement après la décision. Si des renseignements supplémentaires sont demandés et reçus, la décision d’empêcher le chargement de l’envoi est annulée dès que possible.

Shippers who opt to ship and receive cargo through the air cargo supply chain (i.e., shipping on passenger or all-cargo flights), have and retain the right to choose this means from among alternative modes to ship cargo (e.g., by airmail or the marine or land modes (e.g., rail, road)). When a shipper opts to ship via air cargo, there are terms and conditions that apply to this means of shipment, and the contract into which they enter with the air carrier stipulates (pursuant to various conventions) which information is being collected and shared and that the shipment will be subject to all applicable laws that govern the shipment of air cargo. Should a shipment be
denied loading, the shipper can invoke their rights to seek remedies under their contract of carriage or those available under international treaties that govern liability regimes for the shipment of goods on board aircraft. In the case where a PACT decision prevents their cargo from being loaded, they will also be provided contact information for the Program through which they can request an explanation.

answer_value_raw: The premise of the PACT Program (and others like it around the world) is to ensure the continued flow of goods around the globe while adding a layer of security to protect the supply chain from unlawful acts of interference. Using data to perform a risk assessment on a shipment sometimes weeks in advance of loading is widely accepted (see the International Civil Aviation Organization and World Customs Organization's Joint Guiding Principles on Pre-Loading Advanced Cargo Information) to be an efficient and effective means to address potential risk in the least obtrusive means available. In the case of life-saving medical supplies, the supply chain is carefully planned out and follows predictable routes involving known players. Such shipments are also clearly labelled and often have specific handling codes that protect passage from one entity to the next.  This allows for a simplified risk assessment, lessens the chance of shipments being delayed in any way, and in fact facilitates the safe movement of life-saving materials. If life-saving materials were to be prevented from being transported on a specific flight, it would be as a result of a threat item being identified, which if unmitigated, would endanger lives.

answer_text_fr: Le principe du programme CFAPC (et d’autres programmes similaires dans le monde) est d’assurer la circulation continue des marchandises dans le monde entier tout en ajoutant un niveau de sûreté pour protéger la chaîne d’approvisionnement contre les actes d’ingérence illégaux. L’utilisation de données pour effectuer une évaluation des risques sur un chargement, parfois plusieurs semaines avant le chargement, est largement acceptée (voir les principes directeurs communs de l’Organisation de l’aviation civile internationale et de l’Organisation mondiale des douanes sur l’information préalable sur le fret avant le chargement) comme un moyen efficace et efficient de traiter les risques de la manière la moins gênante possible. Dans le cas des fournitures médicales vitales, la chaîne d’approvisionnement est soigneusement planifiée, suit des itinéraires prévisibles et fait intervenir des acteurs connus. Ces envois sont également clairement étiquetés et disposent souvent de codes de manutention particuliers qui protègent le passage d’une entité à l’autre. Cela permet de simplifier l’évaluation des risques, de réduire les risques de retard des envois et, en fait, de faciliter l’acheminement en toute sécurité de fournitures médicales vitales. Si l’on devait empêcher le transport de fournitures médicales vitales sur un vol donné, ce serait à la suite de la détection d’une menace qui, si elle n’est pas atténuée, mettrait des vies en danger.

In addition to providing a secure means of shipping, air carriers are committed to the provision of an expedient service to their clients (including individuals and businesses seeking to ship cargo to Canada). 

Air carriers and data aggregators have been directly involved in the system development to establish a data format and means of transmission that are aligned with industry standards. Dans l’ensemble, le secteur recherche un moyen numérique et transparent d’envoyer de l’information préalable sur le fret et de recevoir des mises à jour et des notifications sur les mesures d’atténuation des risques en temps voulu. En plus de fournir un moyen d’expédition sûr, les transporteurs aériens s’engagent à fournir un service rapide à leurs clients (y compris les particuliers et les entreprises qui cherchent à expédier du fret au Canada).

Les transporteurs aériens et les agrégateurs de données ont participé directement au développement du système en vue d’établir un format de données et des moyens de transmission conformes aux normes du secteur. Une vaste consultation du secteur a été entreprise pendant les projets pilotes de CFAPC depuis 2012 et les points de vue exprimés ont depuis longtemps une influence sur la conception du programme (y compris les paramètres du système). La rétroaction a souligné l’importance de la rapidité dans l’évaluation des risques afin de réduire au minimum les répercussions opérationnelles sur les expéditeurs et les autres partenaires de la chaîne d’approvisionnement.

Les principaux utilisateurs du système (les employés de Transports Canada) ont participé à sa conception et à ses essais afin de s’assurer qu’il est convivial et qu’il répond aux besoins de l’entreprise. C’est-à-dire, un système qui peut recevoir, trier, évaluer le risque et afficher des résultats à partir d’un grand volume de données provenant de diverses sources par l’intermédiaire d’une interface de programmation d’application (API) Web.

L’avantage du système automatisé est l’accélération d’un processus d’évaluation des risques qui ajoute un niveau de sûreté à tous les envois de fret aérien entrant. Les expéditeurs habituels de marchandises légitimes ne devraient pas être touchés par la mise en œuvre du programme de CFAPC. Les transporteurs aériens recevront des mises à jour générées par le système sur les données relatives à leurs envois.

On s’attend à ce que le système permette de multiplier par dix environ le taux de « messages ciblés par heure ». On s’attend également à inclure tous les transporteurs aériens qui desservent le Canada et à évaluer la totalité des données. Actuellement, seuls six pour cent des risques sont évalués à l’aide de méthodes manuelles et sur la base d’un nombre limité de volontaires.

L’évaluation des mesures de protection de la vie privée et de la sûreté appliquées aux référentiels de données qui contiennent les renseignements recueillis, ainsi que le rôle et les contrôles d’accès du personnel de TC chargé de l’exécution du programme de CFAPC, relève également du champ d’application de l’EFVP.

Sous l’effet de modifications apportées au RCSA 2012, les transporteurs aériens sont tenus de soumettre un ensemble de données particulier pour l’ensemble du fret aérien entrant afin de contribuer à la sûreté de ce dernier.

L’automatisation d’une partie des processus de CFAPC permet de collecter, de trier et d’évaluer les risques de toutes les données soumises. Ce taux d’évaluation des risques n’a pas été jugé réalisable sans automatisation.

answer_value_raw: Air carriers submit a mandatory dataset to Transport Canada (shipper and consignee name and address, cargo weight, description and piece count, and air waybill number) and each field is checked for data accuracy (e.g. expected character length, character type, etc.). Specifically, natural language processing and fuzzy matching are used to interpret free text fields in the air waybill to clarify and group the commodity descriptions into meaningful categories (e.g. jeans/denim/pants = clothes). The system then applies an automated risk algorithm that calculates a score. Shipments that fall above a risk threshold are presented for the user for further risk analysis. Targeters review the results and use subject matter expertise to clear the shipment or apply a risk mitigation.

Plus précisément, le traitement du langage naturel et la correspondance floue sont utilisés pour interpréter les champs de texte libre de la lettre de transport aérien. Cela est fait afin de clarifier et de regrouper les descriptions des marchandises dans des catégories significatives (par exemple, jeans/denim/pantalons = vêtements). Le système applique ensuite un algorithme de risque automatisé qui calcule une cote. Les envois qui dépassent un seuil de risque sont présentés à l’utilisateur pour une analyse de risque plus approfondie. Les cibleurs examinent les résultats et font appel à leur expertise en la matière pour autoriser l’envoi ou appliquer une mesure d’atténuation des risques.

Outputs of the system are: an inbound cargo risk score displayed to PACT analysts for each shipment, and electronic messages sent to the air carrier.  

The inbound cargo risk score delineates those shipments that require further review from those that do not. 

The electronic messages let the air carrier know if the data is complete, assessed, or flagged for an RFI, RFS, or a DNL notice. There are two possible automated messages sent by the system when shipment data is received: error codes are sent automatically when incomplete data is received by the system, and assessment complete messages are sent automatically for low-risk shipments once they have been processed by the advanced algorithm. Status messages are sent once a human targeter has made a determination on shipments that fall above the low-risk threshold. These status messages can confirm that the assessment is complete or indicate the need for the air carrier to implement an identified mitigation action.

Les résultats produits par le système se traduisent par une cote de risque pour le fret entrant, affiché pour les analystes de CFAPC pour chaque envoi, et des messages électroniques envoyés au transporteur aérien.

La cote de risque du fret entrant permet de distinguer les envois qui nécessitent un examen plus approfondi de ceux qui n’en nécessitent pas.

Les messages électroniques indiquent au transporteur aérien si les données sont complètes, évaluées ou signalées pour une RFI, une RFS ou un avis DNL. Le système peut envoyer deux types de messages automatisés lorsqu’il reçoit des données sur les envois. Des codes d’erreur sont envoyés automatiquement lorsque le système reçoit des données incomplètes, et des messages d’évaluation complète sont envoyés automatiquement pour les envois à faible risque une fois qu’ils ont été traités par l’algorithme avancé. Des messages d’état sont envoyés une fois qu’un évaluateur humain a pris une décision sur les envois qui dépassent le seuil de faible risque. Ces messages d’état peuvent confirmer que l’évaluation est terminée ou indiquer la nécessité pour le transporteur aérien de mettre en œuvre une mesure d’atténuation établie.

answer_value_raw:
In November 2023, the Canada Student Financial Assistance (CSFA) Program introduced a change to the application verification system that supports the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) called the Repayment Assistance Plan - Enhanced Verification Model (RAP-EVM). 

RAP-EVM is designed to verify the information declared by borrowers, which are all factors in determining RAP eligibility and calculating RAP payment requirements, during the RAP application process (i.e. income, family size and marital status) against taxpayer information provided by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). RAP-EVM applies pre-established business rules to identify applications that meet the selection criteria. Selection criteria were determined using a risk-based sampling methodology to identify high-risk groups more likely to misreport information. The creation of risk group categories was undertaken through statistical analysis of previous cases, in collaboration with ESDC’s Integrity Services Branch. Based on this analysis, CSFA Program identified borrowers with inconsistent family size changes (e.g., if a borrower were to change their response between RAP applications to from a family size of one to a family size above one, and then revert to family size of one), borrowers who claim zero income, and borrowers who report their income just under the RAP zero payment threshold. 

Once selected for verification, a request for taxpayer information (i.e. income, marital status, number of dependants) on these applicants is made to the CRA. If the application data matches CRA taxpayer data, the application is adjudicated for an approval or refusal for RAP. If there are discrepancies, an agent with ESDC’s third-party Service Provider (SP), which operates under banner of the National Student Loans Service Centre (NSLSC), will undertake further verification directly with the borrower. The borrower will then be required to submit additional proof substantiating their information, which an agent will review before making a decision for approval or refusal of the application. 

RAP-EVM replaces the previous, non-authoritative source verification system, which required selected applicants to provide documents to prove that their reported income was accurate; RAP-EVM only requires a borrower to submit additional proof when a discrepancy is identified following the exchange with CRA.

The exchange of borrower and taxpayer information between the SP and the CRA is governed by a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) which outlines the agreement on the information to be exchanged between ESDC and the CRA as well as the conditions and procedures that will apply to the exchange of information. RAP-EVM’s data exchange process between the SP and the CRA is handled via a secure file transfer, known as the Managed Secure File Transfer. Following the exchange of data between CRA and the SP, the RAP application adjudication takes place in a closed environment. Personal information collected and used for the purposes of RAP-EVM is safeguarded under ESDC’s and the CRA’s legal authorities and related policies and directives for collecting and using personal information.    

There are two circumstances under which a borrower may wish to have their RAP decision re-evaluated. Reconsideration is for borrowers that have been refused but can show that unforeseen and unavoidable circumstances have caused them or their spouse or common-law partner to incur exceptional expenses that prevent them from fulfilling their repayment obligations. The other recourse is re-adjudication, which occurs when a borrower has been approved for RAP with a monthly Affordable Payment (AP) but indicates that their gross monthly income has significantly dropped and that they are no longer able to make their AP. 

The Program has completed a Privacy Impact Assessment which was sent to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) in November 2023. Upon review, the OPC recommended that the CFSA Program conduct an Algorithmic Impact Assessment, as the creation of risk group categories in an automated verification process falls within the scope of the Directive on Automated Decision-Making.

Based on this analysis, CSFA Program identified borrowers with inconsistent family size changes (e.g., if a borrower were to change their response between RAP applications to from a family size of one to a family size above one, and then revert to family size of one), borrowers who claim zero income, and borrowers who report their income just under the RAP zero payment threshold. 

Once selected for verification, a request for taxpayer information (i.e. income, marital status, number of dependants) on these applicants is made to the CRA. If the application data matches CRA taxpayer data, the application is adjudicated for an approval or refusal for RAP. If there are discrepancies, an agent with ESDC’s third-party Service Provider (SP), which operates under banner of the National Student Loans Service Centre (NSLSC), will undertake further verification directly with the borrower. The borrower will then be required to submit additional proof substantiating their information, which an agent will review before making a decision for approval or refusal of the application. 

RAP-EVM replaces the previous, non-authoritative source verification system, which required selected applicants to provide documents to prove that their reported income was accurate; RAP-EVM only requires a borrower to submit additional proof when a discrepancy is identified following the exchange with CRA.

The exchange of borrower and taxpayer information between the SP and the CRA is governed by a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) which outlines the agreement on the information to be exchanged between ESDC and the CRA as well as the conditions and procedures that will apply to the exchange of information. RAP-EVM’s data exchange process between the SP and the CRA is handled via a secure file transfer, known as the Managed Secure File Transfer. Following the exchange of data between CRA and the SP, the RAP application adjudication takes place in a closed environment. Personal information collected and used for the purposes of RAP-EVM is safeguarded under ESDC’s and the CRA’s legal authorities and related policies and directives for collecting and using personal information.    

There are two circumstances under which a borrower may wish to have their RAP decision re-evaluated. Reconsideration is for borrowers that have been refused but can show that unforeseen and unavoidable circumstances have caused them or their spouse or common-law partner to incur exceptional expenses that prevent them from fulfilling their repayment obligations. The other recourse is re-adjudication, which occurs when a borrower has been approved for RAP with a monthly Affordable Payment (AP) but indicates that their gross monthly income has significantly dropped and that they are no longer able to make their AP. 

The Program has completed a Privacy Impact Assessment which was sent to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) in November 2023. Upon review, the OPC recommended that the CFSA Program conduct an Algorithmic Impact Assessment, as the creation of risk group categories in an automated verification process falls within the scope of the Directive on Automated Decision-Making.

answer_value_raw:
The following outlines the process flow of RAP-EVM:
1.	Application: The borrower submits their RAP application to the SP, indicating their previous month or current month’s income, married/common-law status and number of dependants. 
a.	On the RAP application, the borrower is informed through their consent that their data can be exchanged with the CRA.

b.	If the borrower has indicated that they are in a married or common-law relationship, then consent, name, date of birth, SIN, and income of their partner will be provided to the SP. A signed consent of the borrower and their spouse must be received prior to any data exchange between the SP and CRA. Spousal signature is a prerequisite for the adjudication of the RAP application.

c.	If the application is complete, SP calculates whether a borrower is eligible for RAP. 

2.	Selection: Those borrowers that have been identified as high risk for misrepresentation based on the risk-based sampling methods may be selected for verification using the RAP-EVM. Borrowers that are not selected for verification are assessed through the regular RAP process, including calculation (#9). RAP calculation precedes selection.

3.	Request for Information: The SP securely sends an electronic request for information to the CRA, including the name, SIN, and date of birth of the borrower and the borrower’s married/common-law partner (if applicable), to confirm previous year’s income (Line 15000 of the borrower’s tax return), marital status, and the number of dependants in the family.

4.	Response to Request: The CRA provides the aforementioned borrower's tax data to the SP.

a.	The response would occur via a secure electronic file transmission.

b.	The response would include the names, date of birth, and SIN of borrowers (and their married/common-law partner, if applicable) as well as their Line 15000 income, number of dependants and marital status. The CRA will also confirm the tax year of the data (the most recent data from the last two years requested only). If the response returns with no data, adjudication process moves to #7.

5.	Data Comparison: The SP compares Line 15000 of the borrower’s income data , as provided by the CRA to the borrower’s reported income on their RAP application. 

a.	Disparities beyond a “threshold of tolerance” in income between a borrower’s CRA tax data and the income declared on the RAP application would justify a request for additional proof from the borrower. The same would apply for inconsistencies with declarations of ‘married’ or ‘single’ and instances where borrowers report a higher number of dependants on their RAP application. The “threshold of tolerance” is determined by the CSFA Program.

b.	The SP annualizes RAP application income data before comparison with CRA borrower (and spouse/common-law partner) income data.

c.	If a family size discrepancy is identified, but the verified family income is less than the family income threshold, additional proof would not be requested since it would not make a difference for adjudication.

6.	Assessment Part One: If the borrower’s declared CRA income, family size and married/common-law status are consistent with the information reported on the RAP application, or if business rules deem no further validation required, the borrower will be assessed for RAP under the existing process.

7.	Assessment Part Two: If there is a variance between their RAP application data and their CRA tax data, or if the CRA is unable to provide the borrower's tax data, the borrower is asked to provide additional substantiating documentation.
8.	Assessment Part Three: Based on the borrower’s declared income and any supporting documentation, the SP proceeds to finalize the assessment of the borrower’s RAP application.

9.	Final Calculation and Decision: The SP runs a final calculation of eligibility, based on verified family income and size, unchanged or revised based on the requested borrower documentation. If the borrower provides additional proof documentation that differs from their RAP application data, their RAP benefit is re-calculated based on the new information.

10.	End of Process: The borrower is informed of the status of their application.

The model assesses data elements in applications submitted to IRCC to triage applications and to automate certain positive eligibility determinations. The model is expected to have little to no impact on the rights and freedoms of individuals as it will solely be used to triage applications and to automate certain positive eligibility determinations. The model rules also only use data elements with a clear link to legislative and regulatory requirements. The model never refuses applications nor does it recommend refusals. All refusals continue to be done by humans as per the current practice. All applications for which eligibility cannot be approved by the model will receive a full individualized assessment by officers in accordance with standard practice, including an officer determining eligibility and screening for admissibility. Officers continue to make the final decision on each application. For applications where the positive eligibility determination is automated by the model, the model determines only that an applicant is eligible, before the application is sent to an officer to screen for admissibility. Even in cases where the model approves the eligibility, officers continue to make the final decision on each application. 

The impact of the triage performed by the model on decision-making officers is limited because officers will not be aware of the rules used by the model for its triage or automated positive eligibility determinations, nor will they receive any information about the analysis that was performed by the model. Further, the model does not produce a recommendation to officers. Each assessment by an officer of an application will be individualized. Model rules were reviewed by experienced officers, legal, policy, data science, and privacy experts, as well as senior decision-makers to ensure they were logical, understandable and aligned with established eligibility criteria. Regular monitoring and quality assurance measures will also help make sure the model continues to perform as intended and that any unforeseen negative impacts such as bias or discrimination can be identified early and mitigated.

The impact of the triage performed by the model on decision-making officers is limited because officers will not be aware of the rules used by the model for its triage or automated positive eligibility determinations, nor will they receive any information about the analysis that was performed by the model. Further, the model does not produce a recommendation to officers. Each assessment by an officer of an application will be individualized. Model rules were reviewed by experienced officers, legal, policy, data science, and privacy experts, as well as senior decision-makers to ensure they were logical, understandable and aligned with established eligibility criteria. Regular monitoring and quality assurance measures will also help make sure the model continues to perform as intended and that any unforeseen negative impacts such as bias or discrimination can be identified early and mitigated.

During the design of the NCL Licensing application, we carefully considered trade-offs between client interests and program objectives to ensure a system that is both efficient and user-friendly while maintaining regulatory integrity. 

One key consideration was balancing the complexity of the system’s design with ease of use. While a more sophisticated system could offer advanced features and greater flexibility, it was essential to ensure that the application process remained accessible to a broad range of users, including those with varying levels of technical expertise. Simplifying the process too much, however, risked limiting necessary functionalities or requiring additional staff intervention, which could reduce overall efficiency. 

Another trade-off involved processing speed versus accuracy. Automation enables faster licence issuance, supporting timely access to spectrum. However, allowing time for applicants to review and correct potential errors was also an important factor. To address this, we designed the system to streamline approvals while incorporating safeguards that enable applicants to rectify mistakes within a reasonable timeframe. 

Additionally, we considered the impact on internal staff. A fully automated system that minimizes user input could place a greater burden on program administrators to validate applications or resolve issues.Conversely, a system with more structured client interactions ensures that applications are submitted correctly, reducing the need for manual corrections and follow-ups. Finding the right balance was key to optimizing both user experience and operational efficiency.

Lors de la conception de l'application de délivrance de LNCL, nous avons minitieusement examiné les compromis entre les intérêts des clients et les objectifs du programme afin de garantir un système à la fois efficace et convivial, tout en préservant l'intégrité réglementaire. 

Une considération essentielle consistait à établir un équilibre entre la complexité de la conception du système et sa simplicité d'utilisation. Bien qu'un système plus sophistiqué puisse offrir des fonctionnalités avancées et une plus grande flexibilité, il était important de veiller à ce que le processus de demande soit accessible à tous les utilisateurs,  quels que soient leurs niveaux d'expertise technique. Toutefois, une simplification excessive du processus pourrait limiter les fonctionnalités essentielles ou nécessiter une intervention supplémentaire du personnel, ce qui pourrait diminuer l'efficacité globale. 

Une autre considération conernait le compromis entre la vitesse de traitement par rapport à la précision. L'automatisation optimise le processus de délivrance de licence, favorisant ainsi l'accès au spectre sous les moindres délais. Toutefois, il était également important de laisser aux requérants le temps pour examiner et de corriger les erreurs potentielles. Pour répondre à cette demande, nous avons conçu le système afin de rationaliser les approbations tout en intégrant des mesures permettant aux requérants de rectifier les erreurs dans un délai raisonnable. 

Également, nous avons examiné l'impact sur le personnel à l’interne. Un système entièrement automatisé, visant à réduire les entrées des utilisateurs pourrait augmenterla charge de travail des administrateurs du programme pour valider les demandes et résoudre les problèmes. Par contre, un système avec des interactions plus structurées avec les clients veille à ce que les demandes soient soumises correctement, réduisantla nécessité de corrections manuelles et de suivis. Il est essentiel de trouver un équilibre pour optimiser à la fois l'expérience de l'utilisateur et l'efficacité opérationnelle.

The system collects and processes various data elements to assess and issue spectrum licences under ISED’s NCL Licensing Framework. Input data is provided directly by applicants through the online application portal, including the requested geographic area (in WKT text or coordinate format), frequency/block requested, technical parameters such as power levels, an attestation of whether they have below or above 100,000 retail mobile phone subscribers and an email for invoicing purposes. No manipulations to the data are made. The system assesses the data by running an automated interference check to assess potential conflicts with existing spectrum users and performing a spectrum cap verification to ensure applicants do not exceed limits based on previously issued licences. This is performed by comparing the data collected to ISED’s radio licence database. Once the initial checks are passed, applications are held in the system for one week to allow for potential review by Spectrum Management Officers (SMO), after which the system automatically generates and sends an authorization email advising the applicant that an invoice will follow. After payment is received, the system automatically issues the licence. The system also automates compliance monitoring by sending up to three reminders (180 days, 90 days and 30 days) to licensees prior to the end of the two-year grace period, prompting them to upload updated site data. This combination of applicant-provided data, system-generated analysis, and ongoing compliance monitoring ensures the licensing process is efficient, transparent, and aligned with program objectives. For the assessment of an application the system produces a number of outputs so that it is clear for applicants as well as Spectrum Management Officers (SMOs). Once an applicant has finished the application process a confirmation of receipt window appears and notifies them an email will be sent with the decision. Decisions in the form of emails are sent to applicants and in the instance where technical or policy considerations have not been met an email with clear reasoning and next steps is sent to the applicant.  Moreover, the applicant has access to a portal that also shows the status of their applications and licences. Post licensing emails are also sent to remind clients to adhere to their conditions of licence as well as related to the payment of a licence and its renewal 

Officers have access to all input data submitted by the applicant, including technical details about the requested spectrum, location, and intended use. This allows them to validate the system’s automated checks if needed. A configurable period is set in the system prior to the licence authorization, allowing officers to inspect and review applications (if needed) as part of continuous quality assurance. Officers are provided with guidance materials and training to ensure they understand the system’s outputs, how to review them, and how to intervene if there are concerns or exceptional cases. This training also covers awareness of potential risks, such as data entry errors or system limitations, and outlines steps for manual review when necessary. Additionally, a series of independent reports are programmed outside the system to complement the system tracking. Among the many transactional reports, a report will be generated daily, flagging to officers any applications that need their attention.

answer_text_fr: Le système recueillit et traite divers données afin d'évaluer et de délivrer des licences de spectre sous le cadre de délivrance de licences de l'ISDE. Les données d'entrée sont fournies directement par les requérants via le portail de demande en ligne, y compris la zone géographique demandée (en format texte WKT ou coordonnées), la fréquence/le bloc de spectre demandé, les paramètres techniques tels que les niveaux de puissance, une attestation indiquant si le nombre d'abonnés au service de détail de téléphones mobiles  est inférieur ou supérieur à 100 000, ainsi qu'une adresse courriel à des fins de facturation. Les données ne sont pas modifiées. Le système procède à une évaluation des données en effectuant un contrôle automatisé du niveau de brouillages afin d'évaluer les conflits potentiels avec les utilisateurs du spectre existants et en vérifiant la limite du spectre afin de s'assurer que les requérants ne dépassent pas les limites en tenant comptedes licences déjà  délivrées. Cette vérification est effectuée en comparant les données collectées avec la base de données des licences radio de l'ISDE. Une fois les vérifications initiales terminées, les demandes sont gardées dans le système pendant une période d’une semaine pour permettre un examen par les AGSs (si nécessaire).  Ensuite, le système génère et envoie automatiquement un courriel d'autorisation informant le requérant qu'une facture suivra. Une fois le paiement reçu, le système délivre automatiquement la licence. Le système automatise également la surveillance de la conformité en envoyant jusqu'à trois rappels aux titulaires de licence avant la fin de la période de grâce de deux ans, pour les inciter à téléverser des données actualisées sur leurs sites. Cette combinaison de données fournies par les requérants, d'analyses générées par le système et de surveillance continue de la conformité assure l'efficacité, la transparence et l'adéquation du processus de délivrance des licences avec les objectifs du programme. Dans le cadre de la politique sur les services et le numérique du gouvernement du Canada, les données relatives aux licences de spectre sont publiées chaque mois sur le site web de l'ISDE.

ISED consulted with ATIP services regarding the requirement for a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) for the Non-Competitive Local (NCL) Licensing Application in February 2022. Following a preliminary review, the ISED delegate for the Privacy Act determined that the NCL Licensing Application was exempt from requiring a PIA. This determination was revisited in 2025, prior to implementation, and was confirmed to remain valid.
A Privacy Protocol is also not required, as the application only collects limited business contact information, which falls under ISED’s Program Participation Class of Record (as published in the annual Info Source report). While the system makes administrative decisions regarding the issuance of spectrum licences, these decisions are typically associated with businesses rather than private individuals. In the rare cases where a licence is issued to an individual, privacy risks are considered very low, particularly given that ISED is required to publicly disclose the names of licence holders.
To ensure transparency and compliance, a TBS-compliant privacy statement was included at the point of information collection, aligning with federal privacy guidelines.

answer_text_fr: ISDE a consulté les services d’AIPRP concernant l’obligation de réaliser une Évaluation des facteurs relatifs à la vie privée (EFVP) pour l’application de licences non concurrentielles locales (LNCL) en février 2022. Bien que le système prenne des décisions administratives concernant la délivrance de licences de spectre, ces décisions sont généralement associées à des entreprises plutôt qu’à des particuliers. Dans les rares cas où une licence est délivrée à un particulier, les risques pour la vie privée sont jugés très faibles, d’autant plus qu’ISDE est tenu de divulguer publiquement les noms des titulaires de licences. Afin d’assurer la transparence et la conformité, une déclaration de confidentialité conforme au SCT a été incluse au moment de la collecte de renseignements, conformément aux lignes directrices fédérales en matière de protection des renseignements personnels.

Automation as a part of the NCL Licensing Framework will analyze data submitted by the applicant and check the following criteria: 1) user-defined area doesn’t exceed area limits 2) interference to and from other applicants/licensees, 3) that the requested bandwidth does not exceed a spectrum cap limit, and 4) that no international coordination might be required if near a border. If an application fails the interference or spectrum cap check, the system generates a detailed rationale and provides recommendations on how to modify and resubmit the application. 

The decision is primarily made by the automated system, with ISED officers having the ability to manually correct errors or review applications if needed. The primary individuals impacted by this decision are applicants seeking a Non-Competitive Local licence. It is estimated that 900 applicants will be affected in the first year, with this number increasing to 3,300 within five years. Given that there are no existing incumbents impacted, the decision primarily affects new applicants who may need to revise and resubmit their applications if they do not initially meet the required conditions. 

The system evaluates data submitted directly by the applicant, including business contact information, business number, requested licence area (WKT format or coordinates), spectrum frequency, spectrum block, and invoicing details. No modifications to the submitted data are made. The system validates applications against established policy requirements, such as maximum licence area size, and ensures that the requested spectrum does not cause interference or exceed allowed bandwidth limits. 

Applicants have recourse options if their application is rejected due to interference concerns or if they have exceeded the spectrum cap limitations. The system provides clear feedback and recommendations, allowing them to adjust the area and/or frequencies and resubmit their application. Applicants will have the ability to edit the area and/or frequencies requested in their application and re-submit it in this case. Although expected to be a rare occurrence, ISED officers are able to manually correct errors that may occur during the licensing process. 

Additionally, the system will automatically authorize the application and send an authorization email to the applicant along with the invoice. Once a full payment is received, the system will generate the licence, which will be available for download in the NCLL portal under the licence account. The system will also facilitate ongoing compliance verification by ensuring that licensees update their station data, as stipulated in the framework. The system will do so by automatically verifying if licensees are updating their station data attesting to their deployment conditions. If the information has not been recorded in the system, reminders will be sent to licensees to inform them to submit the required information, otherwise licenses won’t be eligible for  renewal.

L'automatisation, qui fait partie du cadre de délivrance de LNCL, analysera les données soumises par le requérant et vérifiera les critères suivants : 1) la superficie de la zone définie par l'utilisateur ne dépasse pas les limites de superficies des zones; 2) le  brouillage  avec les licences existantes ou demandes de licence; 3) la largeur de bande demandée ne dépasse pas la limite de  spectre; et 4) qu'aucune coordination internationale ne pourrait être requise pour les superficies situées près de la frontière. Si une demande de licence échoue aux vérifications du niveau de brouillage ou aux limites de spectre, le système génère une explication détaillée ainsi que des recommandations pour faire des changements et de soumettre à nouveau la demande. 

La décision est principalement prise par le système automatisé, avec les agents de l'ISDE ayant la possibilité de corriger manuellement les erreurs ou d'examiner les demandes si nécessaire. Les  personnes principalement concernées par cette décision sont les requérants à la recherche d'une délivrance de licence locale non concurrentielle. Il est estimé que 900 requérants seront concernés la première année, et que ce nombre augementera à 3 300 dans cinq ans. Cette décision impacte principalement les nouveaux requérants qui pourraient devoir réviser et soumettre à nouveau leur demande de licence s'ils ne remplissent pas  les conditions initialement requises. 

 

Le système procède à l’évaluation des informations soumises directement par le requérant, notamment les coordonnées de l'entreprise, le numéro d'identification de l’entreprise, la zone de licence demandée (format WKT ou coordonnées), la fréquence du spectre, le bloc de spectre et les détails de la délivrance des licences. Aucune modification ne sera apportée aux données soumises. Le système vérifie que les demandes respectent les exigences de la politique établie, telles que la limite de superficie de la zone de licence, et   les limites de spectre, ainsi que l’évaluation des risques de brouillage. 

 

Les requérants ont la possibilité de faire des modifications à leur demande si rejetée en raison de problèmes de brouillage ou s’il y a un dépassement de  la limite du spectre. Le système va fournir des informations et des recommandations claires, leur permettant d'ajuster la zone de licence et/ou les fréquences,  et de soumettre à nouveau leur demande. Les requérants auront, par la suite, la possibilité de modifier la zone et/ou les fréquences demandées  et de soumettre à nouveau leur demande. Sur une base exceptionnelle, les agents de de gestion spectre de ISDE ont la possibilité de corriger manuellement les erreurs qui peuvent survenir au cours de la procédure de délivrance des licences. 

 

De plus, le système autorisera automatiquement la demande de licence et enverra un courriel d'autorisation au requérant avec la facture. Après la réception du paiement , le système générera la licence, qui pourra être téléchargée sur le portail de la LNCL sous le compte du requérant. Le système facilitera également la vérification continue de la conformité de la politique en veillant à ce que les titulaires de licence mettent à jour les données relatives à leur station, comme indiqué dans le cadre de délivrance. Pour ce faire, le système vérifiera automatiquement si les titulaires de licence mettent à jour les données de leur station attestant de leurs conditions de déploiement. Si l'information n'a pas été enregistrée dans le système, des rappels seront envoyés aux titulaires de licences pour les informer qu'ils doivent soumettre les informations requises.  À l’absence de ces information,  les licences ne pourront pas renouvellées.

Le système de demande LNCL joue un rôle important dans le processus de prise de décision concernant l'attribution des licences de spectre. Le système intervient à plusieurs étapes essentielles, en commencant avec la soumission de la demande initiale. Il effectue automatiquement des vérifications techniques, par exemple en s'assurant que la zone demandée est dans les limites, que le spectre demandé est disponible, qu'il n'y a pas de potentiel de brouillage et que le requérant ne dépassera pas la limites du spectre dans la zone. Ces contrôles automatisés permettent de s'assurer que les requérants remplissent les conditions d'admissibilité et les exigences techniques de base. 

Après ces vérifications, le système dispose d’une semaine pour permettre aux agents de gestion du spectre (AGS) d'examiner la demande si nécessaire. Cette révision par un agent de spectre constitue un niveau de contrôle supplémentaire,si nécessaire. L'application automatisée pour le cadre de délivrance de licences  LNCL utilise un système basé sur des règles pour évaluer les données d'entrée selon des critères rigoureusement définis, assurant un processus décisionnel transparent, cohérent et efficace. Le système évalue les demandes en fonction de trois critères essentiels : 1) la vérification de la superfiçie de la zone, afin d'assurer que la superfiçie de la zone demandée respecte les limites réglementaires ; 2) l’évaluation du niveau de brouillage, pour assurer que la zone de licence, la largeur de bande ou le bloc demandé ne perturbe pas les titulaires de licences existants ou autres requérants ; 3) la conformité à la limite du spectre, qui permet de vérifier que la zone, la largeur de bande ou le bloc demandé respecte la limite permise par la réglementation. ILa nécessité d'une coordination internationale est également prise en considération lorsque la zone de licence demandée est à proximité de la frontière, mais cela n'affecte pas la délivrance d'une licence.  Ces critères ont été définis conformément aux exigences politiques et réglementaires, aux normes de l’industrie et des lignes directrices techniques en vigeur pour la gestion du spectre.  

Le système évalue principalement la zone de licence sollicitée et la gamme de fréquences ou le bloc de spectre spécifique du requérant. Une fois la demande de licence soumise, le système vérifie automatiquement la zone de licence et le spectre demandé par le requérant avec ceux des licences existantes dans le système de gestion du spectre,  afin d'identifier les conflits potentiels. Il effectue ensuite une analyse du niveau de brouillage pour identifier tout problème technique, vérifie que la largeur de bande ne dépasse pas la limite du spectre autorisé,  et identifie les zones de demande de licence situées proches des frontières internationales qui pourraient nécessiter une coordination supplémentaire. Le système applique des règles  prédéfinies et un processus de validation automatisé pour déterminer si la demande répond aux critères nécessaires. En cas de non-conformité en raison de  matière de brouillage ou de limite du spectre, un rapport sera généré par le système pour expliquer le problème et fournir des recommandations en vue d’une nouvelle soumission. Les requérants reçoivent un retour d'information automatisé, leur permettant d'ajuster leurs demandes et de les soumettre à nouveau sans délais inutiles. 

Une approche similaire basée sur des règles est utilisée dans le processus automatisé de vérification de la conformité, au cours duquel le système vérifie les données téléversées sur le site afin de vérifier si le titulaire de la licence respecte les exigences en matière de déploiement.

answer_value_raw:
Background

Canada’s immigration detention program is governed by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is responsible for monitoring and enforcing conditions imposed on individuals in Canada under the IRPA and the IRPR.

The National Immigration Detention Framework (NIDF) was approved by Parliament in 2016 to create a better, fairer immigration detention system that supports the humane and dignified treatment of individuals while protecting public safety. Immigration detention is based on the principle that detention shall be used only as a measure of last resort, in limited circumstances. In certain cases, however, detention may be deemed necessary when: 
1.	an individual presents a risk to public safety (i.e. when an individual has a documented history or pattern of violent or aggressive crimes/behaviour), 
2.	the CBSA is unable to establish an individual’s legitimate identity, and/or 
3.	the behaviour of the individual threatens program integrity (i.e. such as immigration proceedings or removal). 

When detention must take place, the CBSA uses improved risk assessment processes, developed through the NIDF, to ensure that detainees are placed in the most appropriate facility at the time of detention. 

Several factors must be considered when deciding to detain an individual, including the availability and potential use of all alternatives to detention (ATDs). Over the last eight years, the CBSA has reduced the use of detention by increasing ATDs. ATDs, such as in-person reporting, Community Case Management and Supervision, and Electronic Monitoring, are used to effectively release individuals into the communities while ensuring public safety and immigration program integrity.  

The CBSA has now further expanded ATDs by developing a voluntary smartphone app named ReportIn that allows foreign nationals and permanent residents subject to immigration enforcement conditions to report to the CBSA remotely.

The app uses facial comparison and geographic data to verify the identity and location of individuals.  

The app was developed in compliance with Government of Canada standards on applications for mobile devices.  In addition, feedback from the Privacy Commissioner was included in the development of the app and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) has been completed.  

About ReportIn/CRES
Reporting conditions are imposed by the CBSA, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) or the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) on a case-by-case basis under the IRPA. A common condition imposed is the requirement to report on a regular reporting schedule to the CBSA. The voluntary CBSA ReportIn app will allow individuals subject to reporting conditions to report to the CBSA without physically attending a CBSA office. The ReportIn app will provide a secure process for individuals to report to the CBSA without coming in person to one of our offices while also enhancing the CBSA ability monitor individuals who report remotely.

CBSA CRES/ReportIn solution consists of:
•	A voluntary public-facing smartphone app, ReportIn, where individuals submit reports using a mobile device/smartphone and facial images as a form of authenticating the individuals’ identity. The individuals’ facial biometrics and location, provided by sensors and/or the GPS in the mobile device/smartphone, are recorded when they report through the ReportIn app and is sent to the cloud-based processing and monitoring system, CRES.
•	A Cloud-based processing and monitoring backend system, CRES, allows CBSA immigration enforcement personnel to monitor, contact and assess an individual’s reporting facial images, locations, reporting frequency, and compliance history without individuals having to physically attend a CBSA office.

Using the mobile app, the individual submits photos that are then compared to a reference photo and a similarity score is generated by a facial comparison algorithm. In addition to the automated similarity scoring, CBSA trained staff will review, for every report made by an individual, the submitted photos and a determination will be made whether the submitted photos are a match to the individual. 

The individuals’ location is also collected every time they report and if the individual fails to comply with their conditions. 

ReportIn also allows for one-way CBSA direct messaging with individuals, which will make communication with the individual using the ReportIn app easier.

Other than facial biometric data, the supplemental types of personal information collected by ReportIn includes given and family name, Unique Client Identifier (UCI), personal email address, phone number, employment information (if applicable), facial photos, ad hoc report text, location, device ID, device model, device operating system version, error message, and trace information (where error happened).  

As previously stated, an individuals’ location will be collected and recorded when the following events occur: 
•	When an individual submits their report on their scheduled reporting date, the location, sent by sensors and/or the GPS in the mobile device/smartphone, is recorded when an individual reports through the ReportIn app and is sent to the cloud-based processing and monitoring system CRES. The EnStream location will also be used and connect only to the CRES backend system.  The EnStream service operates externally from and is not connected to the ReportIn app however may be used to collect location when an investigation is opened and the individual has not complied with remote reporting conditions. 

The operational benefits of the project are:
•	Improved management of the inventory of individuals the CBSA must monitor up until they are removed from Canada or the individual becomes a permanent resident of Canada, a Canadian Citizen, granted protected person status in Canada or their temporary resident status is restored. 
•	The ReportIn validation process is much more time efficient than an in-person meeting and provides greater operational flexibility in light of fluctuating volumes of clients.  As such, the ReportIn app is expected to increase monitoring capability while streamlining costs. 

The benefits to the individuals are:
•	Improved communication, transparency and allowing more individuals an alternative to in-person reporting and improving the engagement with the CBSA. 
•	Facilitating a secure process for individuals to enroll and report to the CBSA.
•	Improving support to individuals with accessibility needs where they do not need to attend a CBSA office and providing a more accessible means to report e.g. less time off work, reduced child care cost, reduced transportation cost and/or travel time etc.  

During enrollment the CBSA staff verifies the individual during an in-person or virtual meeting. 

ReportIn uses Amazon Rekognition, a facial recognition software, to perform a comparison of a photo of a known individual against a reference photo. This comparison generates a similarity score, indicating if the individual who is reporting is in fact the individual on reporting conditions.  The software comparison performed is a one-to-one comparison and, to note, is not a one to many comparison. It is also important to note that the software does not compare images against a database of publicly collected images.

All submissions will undergo 100% human oversight. This approach ensures that human judgment and discretion are applied to the results, promoting accountability and accuracy in the system's operation.

There are three levels of review. Background

Canada’s immigration detention program is governed by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is responsible for monitoring and enforcing conditions imposed on individuals in Canada under the IRPA and the IRPR.

The National Immigration Detention Framework (NIDF) was approved by Parliament in 2016 to create a better, fairer immigration detention system that supports the humane and dignified treatment of individuals while protecting public safety. Immigration detention is based on the principle that detention shall be used only as a measure of last resort, in limited circumstances. In certain cases, however, detention may be deemed necessary when: 
1.	an individual presents a risk to public safety (i.e. when an individual has a documented history or pattern of violent or aggressive crimes/behaviour), 
2.	the CBSA is unable to establish an individual’s legitimate identity, and/or 
3.	the behaviour of the individual threatens program integrity (i.e. such as immigration proceedings or removal). 

When detention must take place, the CBSA uses improved risk assessment processes, developed through the NIDF, to ensure that detainees are placed in the most appropriate facility at the time of detention. 

Several factors must be considered when deciding to detain an individual, including the availability and potential use of all alternatives to detention (ATDs). Over the last eight years, the CBSA has reduced the use of detention by increasing ATDs. ATDs, such as in-person reporting, Community Case Management and Supervision, and Electronic Monitoring, are used to effectively release individuals into the communities while ensuring public safety and immigration program integrity.  

The CBSA has now further expanded ATDs by developing a voluntary smartphone app named ReportIn that allows foreign nationals and permanent residents subject to immigration enforcement conditions to report to the CBSA remotely.

The app uses facial comparison and geographic data to verify the identity and location of individuals.  

The app was developed in compliance with Government of Canada standards on applications for mobile devices.  In addition, feedback from the Privacy Commissioner was included in the development of the app and a Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) has been completed.  

About ReportIn/CRES
Reporting conditions are imposed by the CBSA, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) or the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) on a case-by-case basis under the IRPA. A common condition imposed is the requirement to report on a regular reporting schedule to the CBSA. The voluntary CBSA ReportIn app will allow individuals subject to reporting conditions to report to the CBSA without physically attending a CBSA office. The ReportIn app will provide a secure process for individuals to report to the CBSA without coming in person to one of our offices while also enhancing the CBSA ability monitor individuals who report remotely.

CBSA CRES/ReportIn solution consists of:
•	A voluntary public-facing smartphone app, ReportIn, where individuals submit reports using a mobile device/smartphone and facial images as a form of authenticating the individuals’ identity. The individuals’ facial biometrics and location, provided by sensors and/or the GPS in the mobile device/smartphone, are recorded when they report through the ReportIn app and is sent to the cloud-based processing and monitoring system, CRES.
•	A Cloud-based processing and monitoring backend system, CRES, allows CBSA immigration enforcement personnel to monitor, contact and assess an individual’s reporting facial images, locations, reporting frequency, and compliance history without individuals having to physically attend a CBSA office.

Using the mobile app, the individual submits photos that are then compared to a reference photo and a similarity score is generated by a facial comparison algorithm. In addition to the automated similarity scoring, CBSA trained staff will review, for every report made by an individual, the submitted photos and a determination will be made whether the submitted photos are a match to the individual. 

The individuals’ location is also collected every time they report and if the individual fails to comply with their conditions. 

ReportIn also allows for one-way CBSA direct messaging with individuals, which will make communication with the individual using the ReportIn app easier.

Other than facial biometric data, the supplemental types of personal information collected by ReportIn includes given and family name, Unique Client Identifier (UCI), personal email address, phone number, employment information (if applicable), facial photos, ad hoc report text, location, device ID, device model, device operating system version, error message, and trace information (where error happened).  

As previously stated, an individuals’ location will be collected and recorded when the following events occur: 
•	When an individual submits their report on their scheduled reporting date, the location, sent by sensors and/or the GPS in the mobile device/smartphone, is recorded when an individual reports through the ReportIn app and is sent to the cloud-based processing and monitoring system CRES. The EnStream location will also be used and connect only to the CRES backend system.  The EnStream service operates externally from and is not connected to the ReportIn app however may be used to collect location when an investigation is opened and the individual has not complied with remote reporting conditions. 

The operational benefits of the project are:
•	Improved management of the inventory of individuals the CBSA must monitor up until they are removed from Canada or the individual becomes a permanent resident of Canada, a Canadian Citizen, granted protected person status in Canada or their temporary resident status is restored. 
•	The ReportIn validation process is much more time efficient than an in-person meeting and provides greater operational flexibility in light of fluctuating volumes of clients.  As such, the ReportIn app is expected to increase monitoring capability while streamlining costs. 

The benefits to the individuals are:
•	Improved communication, transparency and allowing more individuals an alternative to in-person reporting and improving the engagement with the CBSA. 
•	Facilitating a secure process for individuals to enroll and report to the CBSA.
•	Improving support to individuals with accessibility needs where they do not need to attend a CBSA office and providing a more accessible means to report e.g. less time off work, reduced child care cost, reduced transportation cost and/or travel time etc.  

During enrollment the CBSA staff verifies the individual during an in-person or virtual meeting. 

ReportIn uses Amazon Rekognition, a facial recognition software, to perform a comparison of a photo of a known individual against a reference photo. This comparison generates a similarity score, indicating if the individual who is reporting is in fact the individual on reporting conditions.  The software comparison performed is a one-to-one comparison and, to note, is not a one to many comparison. It is also important to note that the software does not compare images against a database of publicly collected images.

All submissions will undergo 100% human oversight. This approach ensures that human judgment and discretion are applied to the results, promoting accountability and accuracy in the system's operation.

If the ATD MCO is still unable to confirm a facial comparison match, they will refer the case to the Alternatives to Detention Monitoring Centre Supervisor (ATD MCS). If the ATD MCS has additional questions or they are unable to confirm a facial comparison match, they will refer the case to the Regional Inland Enforcement office for investigation by an Inland Enforcement Officer (IEO). If the follow up investigation results in the IEO determining that the individual has not complied with their conditions, the individual could be detained as per the IRPA and IRPR.

The decision that will be automated is the facial comparison portion of the process.**

ReportIn uses Amazon Rekognition, a facial recognition software, to perform a comparison of an individual’s report photo against an individual’s reference photo (known individual) stored in CRES. This comparison generates a similarity score, between the enrollment/reference photo and an individual’s report photo, indicating a percentage similarity score of likelihood that the individual who is reporting is the individual on reporting conditions as indicated by their enrollment/reference photo. The default similarity score for a photo match is 99%.  If a score of under 99% is returned from the software, the result is failed biometrics. If a score of over 99% is returned from the software, the result is passed biometrics. There are several reasons that a result may return at less than 99% and failed biometrics, such as but not limited to, the angle of the face is less than or more than expected, the photo is blurry, the photo is that of another person, etc.

The software analyzes the facial attributes of the face, and then returns a percent similarity score for the face and the facial attributes that are detected in the image e.g. beard, eyeglasses, eyes open, landmarks of the face (e.g. position of nose, mouth).

It is important to note that the software does not compare images against a database of publicly collected images.

All submissions will undergo 100% human oversight by a CBSA employee. This approach ensures that human judgment and discretion are applied to the results, promoting accountability and accuracy in the system's operation.

After the software similarity score is returned and displayed in CRES, each case and/or report is assigned to an ATD MCO to review. The ATD MCO makes the decision on whether or not the report photo is a ‘match’ or ‘no match’. The ‘match’ or ‘no match’ decision is based on the ATD MCO’s determination of the photo match and, when a specified location to report from has been imposed, the individual’s location when they reported. There are three levels of review. All cases and reports will be assigned to an ATD MCO for review. If an individual fails a facial comparison match or location match and the ATD MCO is not able to make a final decision that there is a match, the ATD MCO will contact the individual within a day or two for a follow up investigation. If the ATD MCO still has questions they will refer it to the ATD MCS, if the ATD MCS has additional questions they will refer it to the Regional Inland Enforcement office for investigation by an Inland Enforcement Officer (IEO). If the follow up investigation results in the IEO deciding that the individual has not complied with their conditions, the individual could be detained as per the IRPA and the IRPR.

Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA)
Remote Reporting Program

CRES/ReportIn PIA is has been completed.
The scope of this PIA is to provide an overview of the CRES/ReportIn solution that has been established for the ATD Program, and assess the privacy risks associated with the introduction of the CRES/ReportIn solution.

Specifically, the scope of this PIA includes the following:
•	An overview of the upcoming use of the CRES/ReportIn solution
•	Facial comparison is used as a biometric identifier 

This description includes the following:
•	The systems used to support the CRES/ReportIn solution;
•	CRES/ReportIn events and subsequent activities related to evaluation and assignment of an investigation event in the National Case Management System;
•	The storage, retention and accessibility of CRES/ReportIn data.

In support of efforts to expand and improve ATDs, the CBSA has developed a voluntary smartphone app called ReportIn that allows individuals subject to immigration enforcement conditions to report to the CBSA remotely. Only those individuals expressly required to report to the CBSA as a condition of their release and choose ReportIn as the means of reporting will have access to create an account.

The CBSA will be launching CRES/ReportIn in Fall 2024 on a phased-in basis to provide enough time for the orderly transition of individuals. The app will allow for a reduction in in-person reporting or detention in situations where no current appropriate ATD exists. With the app, the CBSA also has an opportunity to build a more nationally consistent ATD that will be secure and more widely available.

The CRES/ReportIn solution is made up by the following major components: Smartphone Application: Prior to initializing the sign up process, the individual must download the CBSA ReportIn mobile app from either the Apple App store or the Google Play store, based upon the individuals’ device they are using. In order to protect the individuals’ Personal Identifiable Information (PII), a Secure Remote Password (SRP) is used between the individuals’ device and the CRES AWS environment.  Amazon Cognito is used as an authentication provider that supports OAuth 2.0, Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and SRP. The mobile app utilizes AWS Amplify to interface with Amazon Cognito using SRP. Through the Cognito SRP protocol, the mobile app is utilized to implement user sign-up, user sign-in, multi factor authentication and forgot password functionality, minimizing snooping or “Man in the Middle” attack risks.

CRES Web App & Database: The main processing and storage hub for the ReportIn solution is the CRES database, used to store ReportIn individual authentication data, and the web application. The web application is used by the CBSA staff to review and manage the active cases of individuals, as well as providing ongoing as well as historical reporting capabilities. The CRES console is the main interface used by CBSA staff and provides the staff the ability to manage multiple individuals and cases in a centralized location.

Facial recognition software: To validate the individual’s biometric facial data, the app requires the individual to provide multiple biometric facial photos that are used to identify the individual for the duration of their ATD enrollment. The Amazon Rekognition software is used to perform this authentication/validation requirement. The biometric facial photos are hosted in the AWS Government in Canada (GC) Private cloud located within Canadian datacenters to meet data residence requirements.

In 2019, the Canadian Passport Order was amended to authorize the use of automated decision-making, enabling the Passport Program to begin automated processing through the Global Case Management System.  Automated decision-making is only used for routine, low risk cases resulting in positive decisions (e.g. adult passport renewals). Cases that are considered more complex, including all first-time applicants, child applications, and some other cases, will drop out for manual officer review and decision-making. All decisions to refuse, revoke, or cancel a passport will also continue to be made by an officer. 
•	First, the applicant’s identity is verified. 
•	Second, validation of the applicant’s eligibility to a passport is completed, e.g.  to ensure the applicant is a Canadian citizen. 
•	Third, confirmation of the applicant’s entitlement to a passport is completed, e.g.  whether there are any restrictions that could impact the applicant's right to a passport. 
Under the current process for passport renewals, passport officers run a series of manual checks on applications, based on the information that the applicant submits in their application and information available in the system to make a decision on issuance of the passport. The implementation of this automation aims to improve the efficiency of these checks through automated business rules that reflect the manual steps currently performed by a passport officer.

answer_value_raw: Le projet vise à automatiser l’approbation de la recevabilité, pour le répondant et le demandeur principal, des demandes courantes d'époux et de conjoints de la catégorie du regroupement familial à l’étranger. Le projet simplifie également toutes les demandes courantes et standard de la catégorie du regroupement familial à l’étranger en les triant en fonction des caractéristiques communes, afin de favoriser l’efficacité opérationnelle.

answer_value_raw: Un avantage direct pour les clients est que les outils réduisent le délai de traitement « actif » de la recevabilité. Le traitement actif de la recevabilité fait référence au temps que les décideurs consacrent à l’évaluation des demandes de recevabilité. Le délai du traitement actif de la recevabilité de certaines demandes provenant d'époux et de conjoints  de la catégorie du regroupement familial à l’étranger sera réduit, car l’approbation de la recevabilité de certaines demandes sera automatisée. Les outils contribueront indirectement à accélérer les délais de traitement globaux pour les clients.
